evidence_quotes.quote: The WCIDs resisted the political threat to their power over water by advancing a legislative change that permitted WCID governing boards to unilaterally exclude “urban property” (colonias) from their districts.
explore how power over water is challenged through competing legal practices—both legislative changes and the litigation.
The legal process eroded the political foundation on which these communities could claim water.

rationale: Using archival research (legislative files, MALDEF/ACLU legal archives, hearing transcripts, and federal court records), Jepson (2012) conducts a qualitative historical-legal geography case study of two co-central legal mechanisms in South Texas: (1) statutory special-district boundary exclusion/de-annexation and irrigation-versus-domestic mandate demarcation under Texas Article 8280-3.2 (institutional_structure_coordination, primary mechanism), and (2) four years of federal constitutional and Voting Rights Act litigation in Jimenez and Fonseca (review_redress), alongside WCID board electoral participation rules (participation_assistance) and statutory landowner/freeholder candidacy prerequisites and platted/unplatted definitions (eligibility_status_documentation). Because legislative territorial exclusion and federal litigation are co-equally central empirical exposures, assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is 'multiple'. The primary empirical outcome traced across the archival and judicial record is administrative_outcome—specifically, WCID de-annexation resolutions, ballot refusals, federal court dismissals, WCID conversion into narrow Irrigation Districts, and the institutional/governance foreclosure of colonias residents' political standing to claim treated domestic water.
